source: Pleiss, Schiffer, von Weizsaecker (2026) Disentangling generalization and memorization in large language models using chess
finding: Chess move quality of LLMs falls steeply as the density of relevant priors (familiar positions) falls. This is the LLM version of experts being strong only where their stored patterns match.
numbers: Three tiers: within-distribution (WD), near-distribution (ND), out-of-distribution (OOD). Average centipawn loss (ACPL) is 4.75x higher in ND and 7.79x higher in OOD than in WD, across all models. GPT-3.5 ACPL 807.97, GPT-4o 540.38, GPT-5 463.5.
quote: performance consistently degrades as the density of relevant priors decreases
limits: Position familiarity is inferred from opening and engine statistics, not from known training data. One prompt template (FEN in, best move out).
agent_relevance: An agent that leans on recalled patterns fails quietly in unfamiliar states. The schema should detect low pattern match and switch to checked search instead of trusting the first candidate.

source: Pleiss, Schiffer, von Weizsaecker (2026) Disentangling generalization and memorization in large language models using chess
finding: In sparse-prior positions base models fall to random-play level and break the rules. Illegal moves rise sharply with unfamiliarity.
numbers: Illegal-move rate in OOD positions: GPT-3.5 74.7%, GPT-4o 41.6%, GPT-5 33.8%. Claude Opus: ACPL 14.0 with 0.2% illegal (WD), 207.2 with 8.2% (ND), 728.6 with 51.6% (OOD). Gemini: 34.8 with 2.2% (WD), 434.1 with 17.0% (ND), 829.7 with 72.0% (OOD). GPT-3.5, 4o and 5 are worse than random play in all conditions except GPT-5 on WD.
quote: models propose illegal moves at sharply increasing rates
limits: Claude Opus also had 14.4% syntactically invalid output overall, which inflates its numbers. Best-move requests only.
agent_relevance: Humans keep applying fixed rules when patterns fail; LLMs do not. A code-side legality check must sit exactly where pattern cues are weakest.

source: Pleiss, Schiffer, von Weizsaecker (2026) Disentangling generalization and memorization in large language models using chess
finding: More reasoning tokens help, but the relative gain per token shrinks when priors are scarce. Reasoning widens the generalization gap in relative terms.
numbers: GPT-5 ACPL falls 71.74% across conditions with more reasoning: 85.3% (ND), 77.25% (WD), 64.69% (OOD). First reasoning tokens give a 22.55% relative gain in WD, dropping to 7.23% in ND (-67.98%) and 3.81% in OOD (-83.10%). GPT-5 with moderate reasoning is still illegal in over 10% of OOD positions, using about 5x the reasoning tokens of WD.
limits: One model family for the reasoning-effort sweep.
agent_relevance: Extra free thinking does not replace missing patterns. Spend budget on checks in unmatched states, not on longer chains.

source: Pleiss, Schiffer, von Weizsaecker (2026) Disentangling generalization and memorization in large language models using chess
finding: Progress across model generations slows most where patterns are scarce.
numbers: ACPL improvement GPT-3.5 to GPT-4o: 70.7% WD, 35.16% ND, 9.08% OOD. GPT-4o to GPT-5: 69.92%, 10.77%, 5.73%. Overall ACPL reduction 33.12% then 14.23%.
limits: Generations differ in unknown training data.
agent_relevance: Scale alone is unlikely to fix novelty failures. A scaffold that supplies structure for unfamiliar states is the gap to fill.

source: Pleiss, Schiffer, von Weizsaecker (2026) Disentangling generalization and memorization in large language models using chess (citing Reingold and Sheridan 2023)
finding: Human control reported inside this paper: expert and novice chess players doing double-check detection stayed accurate when the notation was unfamiliar. Speed fell, accuracy did not.
numbers: Error rates below 1% for both groups in both notations.
limits: Second-hand: the original study was not opened.
agent_relevance: Humans trade time for accuracy under novelty; LLMs trade accuracy. Budget should buy verification steps.

source: Gobet, Lane, Lloyd-Kelly (2015) Chunks, schemata, and retrieval structures: past and current computational models
finding: CHREST (chunking network plus templates with a fixed core and slots) made a counter-intuitive prediction that was later confirmed: experts should recall random chess positions better than novices, because a large chunk store finds chunks by chance. A verbal rival (long-term working memory) was non-refutable once implemented.
numbers: LT-WM implementation (Gobet 2000): recall ranged from 10 to 100% for both game and random positions depending on parameters. Saariluoma dictation task: over 80% for game positions, no more than 60% for random. Vicente and Wang (1998) argued truly random positions would erase the skill effect; CHREST predicted a smaller but real effect; Gobet and Waters (2003) confirmed it.
quote: not enough constraints are provided by verbal theories
limits: Short opinion article. Little modelling of schemata and retrieval structures exists.
agent_relevance: Build the memory design as a running program with testable predictions, not as a prose idea.

source: Gobet, Lane, Lloyd-Kelly (2015) Chunks, schemata, and retrieval structures: past and current computational models
finding: Chunking networks have been used beyond chess: EPAM-IV for digit span, CHREST for multi-board recall with a retrieval structure, plus syntax, implicit learning, categorisation, agent modelling, and chess problem solving programs (Berliner and Campbell 1984; Gobet and Jansen 1994).
numbers: EPAM-IV digit span: up to 106 digits dictated at 1 per second, 4-level hierarchy (digits, chunks, super-groups, super-group clusters). Gobet (2013): CHREST multi-board recall used the list of chess world champions as retrieval structure.
limits: Brief review; most models were not compared to modern baselines.
agent_relevance: A hierarchy of cores with a retrieval layer scales to long lists; a flat library of templates may not.

source: Gobet and Waters (2003) The role of constraints in expert memory
finding: Template theory was run as CHREST with no fitted parameters and predicted a skill effect on every position type, including truly random ones, shrinking as randomisation grows. Human data matched.
numbers: 16 CHREST nets from 100 to 300,000 nodes, learned from about 50,000 master positions; 500 positions per type, 5 s presentation, visual STM capacity 3. Model vs human fit over 20 points (4 skill groups x 5 position types): r2 = 0.889, RMSD 6.71; r2 = 0.885 without game positions. Model overestimated 1/3-randomised positions by 12.1% and underestimated 3/3 by 3.7%.
quote: TT predicts a skill effect in all position types, including the truly random positions
limits: Humans: N = 36 (7 grandmasters, 12 masters/experts, others down to Class C/D). Skill effect on fully random positions small but reliable. Low power to separate 2/3, random and 3/3 slopes. Age and a limited-fixation strategy also affected random recall.
agent_relevance: A pattern store's benefit shrinks smoothly with match quality. Expected gain from a recalled template should scale with how well it matches.

source: Gobet and Waters (2003) The role of constraints in expert memory
finding: Mechanics of the CHREST template: slots are made only in well-used nodes, and filling a slot is much cheaper than learning a new chunk, so game positions get a big boost that random positions do not.
numbers: Slot rule: more than 3 nodes below share the same piece, square or sub-chunk, and the base node has at least 5 elements. Time costs: familiarisation 2 s, slot fill 250 ms, discrimination too slow for a 5 s presentation. Small nets rarely find templates even in game positions.
limits: Parameters tied to human data in Gobet and Simon (2000). Slot types limited to piece kind, location and chunk.
agent_relevance: Design hint: a stored solution = fixed core + typed slots. Retrieval is cheap when the core matches and fails when only fragments match.

source: Gobet (1993) A computer model of chess memory (Proc. 15th Cognitive Science Society)
finding: Early CHREST, successor of EPAM and MAPP: discrimination net of chunks, STM holding pointers, links between nodes, simulated eye fixations. Simulated random vs game recall and recall of several boards.
numbers: Nets after 230, 1538 and 2843 positions had 630, 2175 and 3646 nodes. Redundant nodes grew slowly: 4 after 100 positions, 10 after 1000, 14 after 2000, 20 after all. Model accounted for 97.4% of Class A players' results in Gobet and Simon experiment 1b and 77.5% in experiment 3; it beat Class A humans at recalling 4 and 5 positions.
limits: Early version, small data, hand-set parameters (STM 20 items while learning, 7 at test).
agent_relevance: A pattern store grows cross-links slowly; a small library is sparse at first, so early benefit is limited to near-exact matches.

source: Ruoss et al. (2024) Amortized planning with large-scale transformers: a case study on chess
finding: A 270M-parameter transformer trained by supervised learning on engine action-values reaches grandmaster-level play with no search. Pattern recognition replaces look-ahead: the machine form of the pattern-recognition theory of search.
numbers: Lichess blitz Elo 2895 vs humans; tournament Elo 2299 (270M), 2259 (136M), 2025 (9M). Puzzle accuracy 95.4% (270M), 94.5% (136M), 88.9% (9M); GPT-3.5-turbo-instruct 66.5%; Leela Chess Zero policy-only 88.6%; Stockfish 16 99.8%. 14.7% of i.i.d. test boards appear in training; under 1.41% of puzzle start boards.
limits: Pattern store distilled from search: 10 million games, 15 billion Stockfish labels. Elo vs bots lower (2299). Distillation not perfect.
agent_relevance: A large verified pattern store can stand in for search on familiar structure. A training-free agent must get the same effect from a retrieved library.

source: Ruoss et al. (2024) Amortized planning with large-scale transformers: a case study on chess
finding: Scaling the stored pattern knowledge helps and is not memorisation: accuracy rises with both data and model size on puzzles that barely overlap training.
numbers: Puzzle accuracy 88.9 (9M) to 95.4 (270M); under 1.41% puzzle board overlap with training.
limits: Same as above.
agent_relevance: If pattern knowledge grows in value with stored examples, a library of verified solved cases should pay off with size, subject to retrieval quality.

source: Karvonen (2024) Emergent world models and latent variable estimation in chess-playing language models
finding: A GPT trained only on real chess game text builds a linear board-state map and also infers a latent player-skill variable. After random opening moves, the model reads the game as low-skill play and does worse; adding a skill vector restores much of it.
numbers: Piece probe accuracy up to 99.6%. Legal-move rate 99.8% (8-layer) and 99.6% (16-layer). Win rate vs Stockfish level 0: 46% (8-layer), 64% (16-layer). On boards after 20 random moves, skill intervention raises win rate 2x (8-layer) and 2.6x (16-layer). Elo probe called 99.4% of 4,000 random-start games low skill.
limits: Small model trained from scratch, not a prompted frontier LLM. Interventions had side effects on neighbouring pieces.
agent_relevance: A model infers the regime from the input and plays accordingly. Telling the agent explicitly which regime it is in (familiar vs unusual) is a testable scaffold.

source: Toshniwal et al. (2022) Chess as a testbed for language model state tracking
finding: Language models trained on move text track piece locations and legal moves with high accuracy given enough data. Adding board-state tokens (random auxiliary pieces, RAP) helps most with small training sets. Full attention over the whole history is needed.
numbers: Legal-move accuracy over 97% for UCI and UCI+RAP. Predicting legal starting squares: 100% with large training, 91.3% with small training. Piece location for a non-moved piece 99.6%. RAP probabilities as high as 50% still improve validation perplexity for small sets.
limits: Trained from scratch, one notation family; prompted frontier LLMs not tested.
agent_relevance: A written board state next to the move list helped weak-data regimes; the analogue is an explicit state summary in the agent loop.

source: Zhu et al. (2023) ChessGPT: bridging policy learning and language modeling
finding: Training on chess games plus commentary gives near-perfect state tracking on real games and a smaller drop on synthetic games. Untuned general LLMs stay weak. This is the only machine-side real-vs-synthetic test found.
numbers: BIG-bench chess state tracking: ChessGPT-Base real short 99.5, medium 97.7, long 98.1; synthetic 94.2, 94.6, 92.8. LLaMA-7B real 29.5, 39.3, 53.0; synthetic 31.3, 39.9, 45.8. Whole-board tracking (UCI to FEN, normalised similarity): baselines under 10%.
limits: Synthetic games are not random-piece positions, so this is a loose analogue of the Chase and Simon random-board test.
agent_relevance: Even a trained model loses several points on unnatural games, and the prompted ones do far worse.

source: Ciancarini and Pareschi (2026) What counts as strategic reasoning? A systematic mapping of chess research on humans, engines, and language models
finding: Map of 84 study families. LLM chess work concentrates on state representation and generalization. Candidate generation is among the least studied stages, so no study found tests pattern-cued candidate moves in LLMs.
numbers: Agent types: human 38 (45.2%), engine 37 (44.0%), LLM 28 (33.3%), neural/RL 24 (28.6%), hybrid 19 (22.6%). Stages: decision 63 (75.0%), assessment 43 (51.2%), evaluation 40 (47.6%), state representation 30, search 24, planning 17, candidate generation 12, reflection 10, explanation 9. In 28 LLM studies: state representation 20, decision 19, assessment 17, search 10, planning 8.
limits: Mapping, not meta-analysis; inclusion and coding are the authors' choices.
agent_relevance: Confirms a literature gap that our scaffold test could fill: does a recalled pattern cue better candidates for an LLM?

source: Yang et al. (2024) Buffer of Thoughts: thought-augmented reasoning with large language models
finding: A meta-buffer of distilled thought-templates is retrieved by embedding similarity between the template description and a distilled problem statement, then instantiated for the task. Closest LLM copy of template retrieval, and it includes chess (checkmate-in-one).
numbers: GPT-4 accuracy %: Checkmate-in-One 36.4 standard, 49.2 ToT, 57.2 meta prompting, 86.4 BoT. Game of 24: 3.0 standard, 74.0 ToT, 82.4 BoT. Geometric Shapes 52.6 to 93.6. Python Puzzles 31.1 to 52.4. Retrieval threshold 0.5 to 0.7; below it the task counts as new.
limits: Authors' own runs; templates come from the same task families, so train-test overlap is close. Limits stated: weak on creativity tasks; a weaker model writes worse templates.
agent_relevance: Copy the loop: describe, retrieve, instantiate slots. Test on unseen task families, which the paper does not.

source: Yang et al. (2024) Buffer of Thoughts, ablations and cost
finding: Removing the meta-buffer or the problem-distiller lowers accuracy most on the hard tasks (Game of 24, Checkmate-in-One). Cost is low because one retrieved template replaces many sampled branches.
numbers: Reported cost 12% of multi-query methods on average. Ablation bars (meta-buffer or distiller removed) show drops largest on Game of 24 and Checkmate-in-One for Llama3-70B and GPT-4; exact bar values not reliably readable from extracted text.
limits: Figures were read from extracted chart text, so exact bars may be misaligned. No test with a retrieval-quality sweep.
agent_relevance: Retrieval of one fitting template can be cheaper than search; the cost saving only holds when a template fits.

source: Suzgun et al. (2025) Dynamic Cheatsheet: test-time learning with adaptive memory
finding: A model that curates a small memory of reusable snippets between questions improves sharply when problems repeat a structure. Strong on Game of 24, but gains are model-dependent.
numbers: GPT-4o Game of 24: 10% baseline, 19% structured prompt with empty memory (DC-), 99% with retrieval and synthesis (DC-RS). Claude 3.5 Sonnet Game of 24: 12% to 14%. Claude AIME 2024 23.3% to 50.0%, AIME 2025 6.7% to 36.7% (DC-Cu). GPQA-Diamond Claude 59.6% to 68.7%; GPT-4o 57.1% to 58.1%.
quote: DC's memory is self-curated, focusing on concise, transferable snippets rather than entire transcripts
limits: AIME sets have 30 questions, so one question is 3.3 points. The Game of 24 jump is one reused Python program, a single pattern and not general skill.
agent_relevance: Closest measured test of stored solution patterns cueing later answers. Win concentrates where a pattern is reusable and cheap to check.

source: Suzgun et al. (2025) Dynamic Cheatsheet, full-history comparison
finding: Dumping every earlier dialogue into context (full history) is worse than curated memory and can fall below the no-memory baseline.
numbers: AIME 2024: Claude full-history 26.7% vs curated DC 50.0%; GPT-4o baseline 20.0%, full-history 6.7%, DC-RS 40.0%.
limits: 30 questions per set; one run per cell as reported.
agent_relevance: A pattern library needs curation and a size cap; raw accumulation hurts, as a novice's unselected memory would.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager: an open-ended embodied agent with large language models
finding: A skill library of executable code, indexed by description embeddings and retrieved top-5 from plan plus environment feedback, lets the agent build harder skills on older ones and reuse them in a fresh world.
numbers: 63 unique items in 160 iterations, 3.3x the baselines. Tech tree: wooden 15.3x, stone 8.5x, iron 6.4x faster; only agent to reach diamond. Zero-shot to four unseen tasks in a new world: Voyager solves all, baselines none within 50 iterations. Skill retrieval (309 samples): top-1 80.2 +- 3.0, top-2 89.3, top-3 93.2, top-4 95.2, top-5 96.5 +- 0.3.
quote: ever-growing skill library of executable code
limits: Minecraft only, GPT-4 code generation. Selection is by description similarity, not structure.
agent_relevance: Offer a few cued candidates (top-5 is 96.5% vs 80.2% for top-1) and let code check them, rather than commit to one recalled pattern.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager, ablations
finding: Without the skill library progress plateaus late; the biggest losses came from removing curriculum and self-verification.
numbers: Random curriculum: discovered items down 93%. No self-verification: down 73%. No skill library: plateaus in later stages (figure only, no exact figure in text).
limits: Ablations over a small number of runs, read from a figure.
agent_relevance: A cued pattern library helps most late, when tasks compose earlier ones. Verification mattered more than recall.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Agent Workflow Memory
finding: Agents induce reusable workflows from past successes and supply them selectively. Induction on test queries helps most under distribution shift.
numbers: WebArena success 35.5% vs 23.5% autonomous BrowserGym baseline (+12.0 points, 51.1% relative). Mind2Web step success cross-task: MindAct 36.2 vs AWM offline 45.1 and online 43.6; cross-website 30.1 vs 33.7 / 33.9; cross-domain 18.6 vs 32.6 / 35.5. Gaps grow with shift by 8.9 to 14.0 points.
limits: Whole-task success on Mind2Web stays about 1 to 5%. Wrongly induced workflows degrade results. GPT-4 only.
agent_relevance: Reusable cores transfer, but core quality caps the gain. Online induction handles drift better than a fixed library.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM agents are experiential learners
finding: Abstract insights and retrieved similar trajectories are complementary. Rule-like insights suit analysis tasks, trajectories suit action tasks. Insights transfer across tasks.
numbers: HotpotQA insights-only 36% vs retrieval-only 31%; ALFWorld 50% vs 55%; WebShop 37% vs 38%. HotpotQA to FEVER transfer: ReAct 58, ExpeL transfer without task demos 63 +- 0.4, ExpeL transfer 70 +- 0.7 (row order follows the paper's table). ALFWorld with Reflexion rounds R0 to R3: retrieve-only 40.3 to 54.4, ExpeL+Reflexion 54.5 to 60.4 (middle rows).
limits: Table text was garbled in extraction, so row labels for some cells are inferred from table order. Small environments.
agent_relevance: Two memory forms (abstract core and concrete case) mirror chunk vs template. Task type decides which cue wins.

source: Provenzano et al. (2026) EvoSkill: automated skill discovery for multi-agent systems
finding: Skills evolved from failure analysis and kept only if they raise held-out validation score improve accuracy with a frozen model and transfer to another benchmark.
numbers: OfficeQA exact match 60.6% to 67.9% (+7.3). SealQA 26.6% to 38.7% (+12.1). SealQA skill on BrowseComp 43.5% to 48.8% (+5.3). Training fractions 5/10/15% (12, 24, 36 examples): 63.4, 65.8, 64.5 exact match, plateau after 10%.
limits: Small sets, one agent setup (Claude Code with Opus 4.5), transfer shown for one pair.
agent_relevance: Few examples suffice for a useful skill, and held-out checking fits our rule G3. More examples did not help.

source: SoK: Agentic skills beyond tool use in LLM agents (2026)
finding: Survey of the skill lifecycle. Reports that curated skills beat self-generated ones, flags retrieval precision versus recall as the core tension, and documents supply-chain risk.
numbers: Cites SkillsBench: curated skills raise pass rates by 16.2 points on average; self-generated skills lower them by 1.3 points. About 1,200 malicious skills infiltrated one marketplace.
limits: The benchmark figures are cited second-hand; SkillsBench itself was not opened.
agent_relevance: A pattern enters the library only after external evidence. Self-written patterns without checks can be neutral or harmful.

source: Yang et al. (2025) ReasonFlux: hierarchical LLM reasoning via scaling thought templates
finding: A library of about 500 high-level thought templates plus reinforcement learning on template sequences gives a 32B model strong math scores.
numbers: MATH 91.2%, 6.7 points above o1-preview; AIME 2024 56.7% as stated in the abstract.
limits: Trained, not scaffold only. Abstract and top results table read; ablations not studied.
agent_relevance: Template libraries scale to hundreds of items in math, though here the gain is bought with training.
